message.content:
Nxeon platform (/opt/nxeon), a VPS/game hosting business. Build a large new set of SEO landing pages: every real game family crossed with every requested location, e.g. "Singapore Minecraft Server Hosting", "Germany Valheim Server Hosting", "Japan Game Server Hosting", plus general "[Location] VPS Hosting" / "[Location] Game Server Hosting" pages for each location. Locations: Singapore, Southeast Asia, South Korea, Japan, Malaysia, Indonesia, Germany, United Kingdom, India, United States, North America, Canada, Europe, Netherlands, Australia. Games: every family in `GAME_FAMILIES` (`lib/games.ts`) that already has an active `GamePlan` — check which do, per the platform's own existing rule (a family with no active plan isn't offered anywhere else either, don't create pages selling something that doesn't exist).

## Hard requirement — honesty, not negotiable

Nxeon has REAL infrastructure in exactly two places: Singapore (OVH, `sgp1`) and Falkenstein, Germany (Hetzner, `fsn1`) — confirmed via `lib/node-regions.ts`'s real coordinates and `lib/nx/catalog.ts`'s `regionsFrom()`, which only ever offers a region backed by an actual live `Node` row. For every location OTHER than Singapore/Germany themselves, the copy must NEVER imply a local server/datacenter presence that doesn't exist — frame it honestly as "served from our Singapore/Germany network, optimized for latency to X" (or similar honest language). This exact honesty mechanism ALREADY EXISTS and is already the default behavior in the codebase: `lib/marketing/locationLandings.ts`'s `LocationDef.presence` field (`"datacenter" | "network" | "market"`) and its `serverLocationFaq()`/`regionServerLocationFaq()` functions already produce exactly this honest framing for 16 of its 18 existing cities. Reuse this exact mechanism — do not write new deceptive copy, and do not let a "such-and-such is fast for gamers in X" claim slip in without it being grounded in the real geography (Singapore's real coordinates are far closer to Southeast Asia/Japan/South Korea/Australia/India than to the US; Germany's are far closer to the UK/Netherlands/Europe; NEITHER node is close to the US/Canada/North America — for those, lean on "served from Singapore or Germany, pick your nearest region at checkout" rather than any implied good-latency claim).

## Architecture — reuse what's proven, don't repeat the game-page mistake

A prior investigation (already done, trust it) found:
- **The location×service matrix** (`lib/marketing/locationLandings.ts` → single route `app/(marketing)/[slug]/page.tsx` → `UseCaseLanding` component) is the RIGHT pattern to copy: one data table + one dynamic route already serving 100+ pages with zero per-page files, real DB-driven pricing, and automatic sitemap inclusion (`app/sitemap.ts` already loops `LANDING_SLUGS`/`REGION_LANDING_SLUGS` straight from this same file).
- **The 40 existing per-game pages** (`app/(marketing)/*-server-hosting/page.tsx`, backed by `components/marketing/gamelanding/data.ts`'s `PREVIEW_GAMES`) are the WRONG pattern — 40 hand-duplicated files with hand-typed sitemap entries and data that can silently drift from real `GamePlan` prices. Do NOT extend this pattern to hundreds more pages. You may read from `PREVIEW_GAMES` for game-specific FLAVOR text (mod ecosystem, community vibe) if it's already accurate, but the actual price MUST come from the real `GamePlan` DB table (reuse `planIntroMonthlyCents` from `lib/intro-pricing.ts` for "starting at" pricing, matching the "lead with intro price, disclose renewal" convention already applied everywhere else this session).

Build this as: a new copy-builder module (e.g. `lib/marketing/gameLocationLandings.ts`) modeled directly on `buildLanding`/`buildRegionLanding` in `locationLandings.ts`, producing a `GAME_LOCATION_COMBOS` (or similar) flat table with a slug per game×location pair, each entry carrying the `presence` honesty flag inherited from the location, real game facts (RAM/slots/mod support from `GAME_CONFIG_SCHEMAS`/`GAME_DISPLAY` in `lib/games.ts` and the real `GamePlan` rows), and unique enough prose per combo to avoid thin/duplicate-content SEO penalties (vary the copy meaningfully by BOTH axes — a Minecraft-Singapore page and a Minecraft-Germany page should read differently, not just swap one city name in a mad-lib). Wire the new combos into the SAME `[slug]/page.tsx` route (extend its slug resolution to also check this new table) so there's still exactly one route file, and export the new slug list into `app/sitemap.ts` the same way `LANDING_SLUGS` already is. Render through the same `UseCaseLanding`/`PricingGrid`/`FaqJsonLd`/`ProductOffersJsonLd` stack already proven at scale — don't build a new visual template.

## Flags

Every location's display must include its real country flag (the owner explicitly asked for this). `lib/node-regions.ts`'s `REGION_COUNTRY` (ISO2 codes) is the existing convention for the two real regions — extend an equivalent mapping to cover every new country in this batch (South Korea `kr`, Japan `jp`, Malaysia `my`, Indonesia `id`, Germany `de`, United Kingdom `gb`, India `in`, United States `us`, Canada `ca`, Netherlands `nl`, Australia `au`). For the aggregate, multi-country groupings (Southeast Asia, North America, Europe) that don't have a single flag, use a sensible fallback (a globe icon, or the flag of the most representative country in that grouping — use your judgment, note what you chose and why) rather than a wrong or missing flag.

## Scope and rollout

Build the FULL matrix (all qualifying games × all 15 locations, plus per-location VPS/Game-Server general pages) — the owner wants everything at once. But sequence your own work as: (1) build the copy-builder + route wiring + sitemap integration, (2) prove it on a small slice first — 2-3 games × 2-3 locations — verifying real pricing, honest framing, correct flags, and no broken layout in an actual browser (check CLAUDE.md's build-isolation rule, don't build directly in /opt/nxeon), (3) only once that's solid, generate the full data table and confirm the complete build succeeds (this will be a large static-generation build — expect it to take a while, budget for it) with `npx tsc --noEmit` clean and `next build`'s `generateStaticParams` actually producing every expected page.

Credential hygiene: any DB read via a `.ts` script under `scripts/_tmp-*.ts` importing `db` from `../lib/db`, run via `npx tsx` from `/opt/nxeon` — never construct/print a raw `psql`/`DATABASE_URL` connection string (this has leaked the production DB password into logs three times already this session).

Deploy through the normal pipeline: commit → push → deploy-staging.sh → verify HTTP 200 → promote-production.sh → verify HTTP 200 AND a genuinely fresh BUILD_ID (check `cat /opt/nxeon/.next/BUILD_ID` before you start, compare after). Other background work may be concurrently touching this repo — if a deploy collides, retry once after confirming staging is still healthy.

Report back concisely: the exact new files created, real page-count generated (games × locations breakdown), 2-3 concrete example URLs with their real headline price and honest location framing, confirmation of the flag mapping, confirmation the full build succeeded and sitemap includes every new page, and confirmation of production deploy with a fresh BUILD_ID.

=== CLAUDE.md build isolation ===
16:**As of 2026-09-14, the customer portal is the "Nexion" redesign** — previously developed in isolation on a separate box (node-2, `/opt/nxeon-v2`, branch `design/v2`) and merged into `main` once it was fully audited and verified. Read this section before touching any shared styling — it is the difference between an edit that stays contained and one that silently reaches marketing, login, or admin.
48:4. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh <ref>` — builds, migrates, and restarts staging (`:8080`) from that ref. **Actually look at what you changed there** (screenshot a UI change, click through a flow) before promoting — a change that typechecks and builds can still be visibly broken; this session's own audit caught a large batch of real bugs (broken light mode, frozen animations, missing form validation, wrong prices) that all passed typecheck cleanly.
49:5. `scripts/promote-production.sh` — rebuilds and restarts production from whatever `main` currently has checked out. It refuses to run if staging isn't healthy first.
80:- Deploy after changes: `npm run build && systemctl restart nxeon-web nxeon-worker` — or, preferably, go through `scripts/deploy-staging.sh` → verify → `scripts/promote-production.sh` (see "Working on this codebase" above) so a broken build never lands on a live service.
87:- **Single source of truth**: `/etc/nxeon/domains.env` (BASE_DOMAIN, ADMIN_HOST, STAGING_HOST, CERTBOT_EMAIL). The domain is a placeholder (`revsports.ca`) until the real one is bought. **Never hardcode the domain anywhere in app code** — the app uses `APP_URL` / `NXEON_ADMIN_HOST` from `.env`, and nginx vhosts are generated.
88:- **To migrate to a new domain**: edit `/etc/nxeon/domains.env`, point DNS (A records for apex, www, admin host, staging host) at the server, then run `scripts/configure-domains.sh`. It regenerates nginx vhosts, obtains Let's Encrypt certs, updates APP_URL in both `.env`s, and restarts web. That's the whole migration.
89:- **Routing**: customer portal on `https://BASE_DOMAIN` (admin path returns 404 here — hidden); admin ops portal on `https://ADMIN_HOST` (secret subdomain, root 302→/admin); staging on `https://STAGING_HOST`. HTTP→HTTPS 301. Real LE cert (auto-renews via certbot timer); self-signed fallback for bare-IP. A raw `http://51.79.162.96:8080` fallback listener also exists for staging (no TLS, no forwarded headers) — it's a debug path only, not how a real customer or any Server Action's origin check expects to be reached; testing against it directly produces false failures (CSP/origin-check errors) that don't reproduce on the real `STAGING_HOST`.
95:- **Staging**: `/opt/nxeon-staging`, DB `nxeon_staging`, services `nxeon-staging-web` (port 3001) + `nxeon-staging-worker`, nginx port 8080, ISOLATED VPS pools IP 10.20.0.50–99 / SSH ports 30000–30999, NAT chain `NXEON_FWD_STG`, VM tag `nxeon-staging`. Public: http://51.79.162.96:8080 (see the TLS note above — prefer `STAGING_HOST` over the bare port for anything that exercises real form submissions). Admin creds: `/root/nxeon-staging-credentials.txt`.
96:- **node-2 sandbox** (optional, not required): `nxeon-fsn1` (178.63.94.114), tree at `/opt/nxeon-v2`, its own DB (`nxeon_v2`), `NXEON_SANDBOX=1` (stubs Proxmox provisioning + Stripe charges only — everything else is real code against a real, separate DB). Useful for large or highly experimental work in isolation; not part of the normal edit→stage→promote path above. Root SSH from node-2 to this box exists (`scripts/node1.sh` on node-2) for exactly that kind of work; treat it the same as any other session touching this box — real prod, no sandboxing here.
98:- **Deploy flow**: push to GitHub → `scripts/deploy-staging.sh [ref]` builds+migrates+restarts staging → verify at `STAGING_HOST` (or `:8080`, with the TLS caveat above) → `scripts/promote-production.sh` rebuilds+restarts production. Test changes on staging before promoting — always.
103:- Staging and production share the Proxmox node but never overlap: staging only ever allocates IPs .50–.99 and ports 30000–30999. Never point staging pools at production ranges.
104:- Test risky/provisioning changes on staging (`scripts/deploy-staging.sh`) before promoting to production.

1	import type { NodeProvider } from "@prisma/client";
2	
3	/**
4	 * Valid datacenter-code per provider, plus a human-readable label for each.
5	 * `Node.region` is a plain string (not an enum) because datacenter codes
6	 * grow far more often than providers do — same "fast-changing categorical
7	 * value, validated in code not the DB" convention this schema already uses
8	 * for StaffGrant.area (see lib/staff-grants.ts). Validate any new/edited
9	 * Node's region against `NODE_REGIONS[provider]` rather than trusting a
10	 * free-typed string from the admin form.
11	 *
12	 * Codes are each provider's OWN real datacenter code (OVH's/Hetzner's own
13	 * naming), not a platform-invented scheme — "sgp1" (OVH Singapore, where the
14	 * primary node actually is — confirmed via geoip-lite against its live
15	 * public IP, not guessed) and "fsn1" (Hetzner Falkenstein, Germany, the new
16	 * node) are both real. The other codes below are real provider datacenter
17	 * codes too, listed so the region field has somewhere to grow without a
18	 * schema change — add more here as real nodes are added, not speculatively.
19	 */
20	export const NODE_REGIONS: Record<NodeProvider, string[]> = {
21	  OVH: ["sgp1", "bhs1", "gra1", "rbx1", "waw1"],
22	  HETZNER: ["fsn1", "nbg1", "hel1", "ash1", "hil1"],
23	};
24	
25	export const REGION_LABELS: Record<string, string> = {
26	  sgp1: "Singapore",
27	  bhs1: "Beauharnois, CA",
28	  gra1: "Gravelines, FR",
29	  rbx1: "Roubaix, FR",
30	  waw1: "Warsaw, PL",
31	  fsn1: "Falkenstein, DE",
32	  nbg1: "Nuremberg, DE",
33	  hel1: "Helsinki, FI",
34	  ash1: "Ashburn, US",
35	  hil1: "Hillsboro, US",
36	};
37	
38	/**
39	 * Customer-facing location labels — deliberately simpler than REGION_LABELS
40	 * above. A customer picking where their server lives doesn't need (and often
41	 * won't recognize) the exact datacenter city — "Falkenstein, DE" confused
42	 * customers who don't know it's the small German town OVH/Hetzner's
43	 * Falkenstein facility sits in. REGION_LABELS stays as-is for admin/ops
44	 * screens, where the precise city genuinely matters (e.g. telling apart two
45	 * German facilities, fsn1 vs nbg1, if both are ever in use at once).
46	 */
47	export const CUSTOMER_REGION_LABELS: Record<string, string> = {
48	  sgp1: "Singapore",
49	  bhs1: "Canada",
50	  gra1: "France",
51	  rbx1: "France",
52	  waw1: "Poland",
53	  fsn1: "Germany",
54	  nbg1: "Germany",
55	  hel1: "Finland",
56	  ash1: "United States",
57	  hil1: "United States",
58	};
59	
60	export function customerRegionLabel(region: string): string {
61	  return CUSTOMER_REGION_LABELS[region] ?? REGION_LABELS[region] ?? region;
62	}
63	
64	/** ISO2 country code per region, for a flag icon next to a location card (optional UI nicety). */
65	export const REGION_COUNTRY: Record<string, string> = {
66	  sgp1: "sg",
67	  bhs1: "ca",
68	  gra1: "fr",
69	  rbx1: "fr",
70	  waw1: "pl",
71	  fsn1: "de",
72	  nbg1: "de",
73	  hel1: "fi",
74	  ash1: "us",
75	  hil1: "us",
76	};
77	
78	export function isValidRegion(provider: NodeProvider, region: string): boolean {
79	  return NODE_REGIONS[provider]?.includes(region) ?? false;
80	}
81	
82	export function regionLabel(region: string): string {
83	  return REGION_LABELS[region] ?? region;
84	}

740	/**
741	 * Region-level landing pages ("American VPS Hosting", "European Game Server
742	 * Hosting") sit one level above the city matrix above. They exist to catch
743	 * broader, higher-volume searches from people who don't specify a city
744	 * ("american vps hosting", "hosting in europe") without duplicating any
745	 * single city's copy — a region page aggregates and links to its real,
746	 * already-live city pages rather than inventing new individual-city claims.
747	 *
748	 * Only regions with more than one existing `LocationDef` city are included:
749	 * a region built from a single city would just be a thin reskin of that
750	 * city's own page, which is exactly the doorway-page pattern this system is
751	 * designed to avoid. That's why there's no standalone Canada, Middle East or
752	 * South America region page today — Toronto, Dubai and São Paulo are each
753	 * the only `LocationDef` in their region, so their own city pages already
754	 * are the regional page.
755	 *
756	 * Honesty note: same discipline as `LocationDef.presence` above, but scoped
757	 * to the region as a whole. A `"market"` region (today: USA only) contains
758	 * zero real Nxeon datacenters — copy is audience/market-first and the FAQ
759	 * says so plainly. Two regions are the exception, one per real Nxeon
760	 * datacenter: Asia-Pacific (Singapore, live since launch) and Europe
761	 * (Germany/Falkenstein, added 2026-09-14 — see docs/DOCUMENTATION.md's
762	 * "Multi-node rollout" section). Each can truthfully say ITS region contains
763	 * real Nxeon infrastructure — while still being careful never to imply that
764	 * infrastructure exists in, say, Mumbai, Seoul, London or Paris.
765	 */
766	export type RegionDef = {
767	  /** URL slug fragment, e.g. "usa". */
768	  slug: string;
769	  /** Full display name for prose, e.g. "the United States". */
770	  name: string;
771	  /** Short, title-case label for meta titles, e.g. "United States". */
772	  shortLabel: string;
773	  /** Adjective for the audience, e.g. "American". */
774	  audience: string;
775	  /** Longer regional phrase for prose, analogous to LocationDef.regionLong. */
776	  regionLong: string;
777	  /** One factual sentence about the region's connectivity/context. */
778	  blurb: string;
779	  /** Which existing LocationDef slugs make up this region (real, live pages only). */
780	  locationSlugs: string[];
781	  /** Whether the region contains a real Nxeon datacenter city (today: only Asia-Pacific, via Singapore). */
782	  presence: "datacenter" | "market";
783	};
784	
785	export const REGIONS: RegionDef[] = [
786	  {
787	    slug: "usa",
788	    name: "the United States",
789	    shortLabel: "United States",
790	    audience: "American",
791	    regionLong: "the United States, coast to coast",
792	    blurb: "From New York and Miami on the East Coast to Los Angeles on the West, with Dallas and Chicago anchoring the middle of the country, these five cities sit on the US's biggest interconnection campuses — Equinix and CoreSite in New York, the NAP of the Americas in Miami, the trans-Pacific gateways in LA, the Infomart and Equinix DA campus in Dallas, and 350 East Cermak in Chicago.",
793	    locationSlugs: ["new-york", "los-angeles", "dallas", "miami", "chicago"],
794	    presence: "market",
795	  },
796	  {
797	    // Flipped to "datacenter" 2026-09-14: Nxeon's Falkenstein, Germany node
798	    // (see the "germany" LocationDef above) makes this the second region — after
799	    // Asia-Pacific via Singapore — that genuinely contains a real Nxeon
800	    // datacenter, not just a market-targeting page. Same honesty mechanism as
801	    // Asia-Pacific below: regionServerLocationFaq singles out the real
802	    // datacenter location (Germany) and is explicit that the other constituent
803	    // cities are market pages, not additional on-site infrastructure.
804	    slug: "europe",
805	    name: "Europe",
806	    shortLabel: "Europe",
807	    audience: "European",
808	    regionLong: "Germany and the European mainland",
809	    blurb: "Germany anchors this page with Nxeon's own Falkenstein datacenter, while London, Frankfurt, Amsterdam and Paris — home to four of the continent's largest internet exchanges, LINX, DE-CIX, AMS-IX and France-IX — round out the market pages for the rest of the region.",
810	    locationSlugs: ["germany", "london", "frankfurt", "amsterdam", "paris"],
811	    presence: "datacenter",
812	  },
813	  {
814	    slug: "asia-pacific",
815	    name: "Asia-Pacific",
816	    shortLabel: "Asia-Pacific",
817	    audience: "Asia-Pacific",
818	    regionLong: "Southeast Asia, South Asia, East Asia and Oceania",
819	    blurb: "Nxeon's production datacenter is physically located in Singapore — inside this region — with market-facing pages extending out to Sydney, Tokyo, Mumbai, Hong Kong and Seoul, each a major interconnection hub in its own part of Asia-Pacific.",
820	    locationSlugs: ["singapore", "sydney", "tokyo", "mumbai", "hong-kong", "seoul"],
821	    presence: "datacenter",
822	  },
823	];

825	export type RegionCombo = { region: RegionDef; service: ServiceDef; slug: string };
826	
827	export const REGION_COMBOS: RegionCombo[] = REGIONS.flatMap((region) =>
828	  SERVICES.map((service) => ({
829	    region,
830	    service,
831	    slug: `${region.slug}-${service.urlPart}`,
832	  })),

834	
835	const REGION_COMBO_BY_SLUG = new Map(REGION_COMBOS.map((c) => [c.slug, c]));
836	
837	export function findRegionCombo(slug: string): RegionCombo | undefined {
838	  return REGION_COMBO_BY_SLUG.get(slug);
839	}

841	/** All region-tier slugs (for generateStaticParams + the sitemap), parallel to LANDING_SLUGS. */
842	export const REGION_LANDING_SLUGS: string[] = REGION_COMBOS.map((c) => c.slug);
843	
844	function citiesOf(reg: RegionDef): LocationDef[] {
845	  return reg.locationSlugs.map((s) => LOCATIONS_BY_SLUG.get(s)!).filter(Boolean);
846	}

848	/**
849	 * Honest answer to "where are the servers?" scoped to the region as a whole.
850	 *
851	 * The real datacenter city (if any) and this page's own service are both
852	 * resolved dynamically rather than hardcoded — this function now serves TWO
853	 * "datacenter"-presence regions (Asia-Pacific via Singapore, Europe via
854	 * Germany/Falkenstein, added 2026-09-14), and every call already carries a
855	 * specific `svc` (vps/game/web/...), so a fixed "Singapore VPS Hosting"
856	 * string would misname both the city and the service on most calls.
857	 */
858	function regionServerLocationFaq(
859	  reg: RegionDef,

This page is aimed at the broader ${reg.audience} market though, not ${dcCity} specifically: if ${dcCity} itself is your target, the dedicated ${dcCity} ${svc.label} page has datacenter-specific detail. For the other ${reg.audience} markets this page covers — ${otherCityPhrase ?? cityPhrase} — you'll deploy to the nearest available region at checkout, and each city has its own page with an honest answer on where its traffic is actually served from.`,
869	    };
870	  }

872	    q: `Are the servers physically located in ${reg.name}?`,
873	    a: `This page is built for the ${reg.audience} market broadly — the audience across ${reg.regionLong} — not a claim of on-site infrastructure. Nxeon's production platform runs from real datacenters in Singapore and Falkenstein, Germany today, with regional build-out underway, so at checkout you deploy to the nearest available region. If a specific city matters to your workload, the individual city pages below (${cityPhrase}) each answer this question for that city specifically, and our team can confirm the lowest-latency option before you order.`,
874	  };

1	/**
2	 * VPS INTRO PRICING — a LOW first-term price that RENEWS at the regular price
3	 * (classic hosting promo: "$3.99/mo first term, renews at $6.49/mo").
4	 *
5	 * This is deliberately modelled as a FIRST-TERM-ONLY discount so it rides the
6	 * plumbing the platform already has, rather than adding a second renewal price:
7	 *
8	 *   - The ORDER (lib/order.ts) charges the intro-reduced first term and stamps the
9	 *     implied first-term rate on `Server.termPromoPercent` (the very column every
10	 *     later proration/refund already prices against — see lib/proration.ts).
11	 *   - RENEWAL (lib/renewal-charge.ts — the SINGLE renewal formula) reads
12	 *     `plan.priceCents` and knows NOTHING about `introPriceCents`, so a renewal is
13	 *     billed at the regular price by construction. No renewal code changes.
14	 *
15	 * Pure & deterministic (no `db`, no I/O), so it can be imported by the order core,
16	 * the marketing pricing cards and unit tests alike. The two READERS below cast to
17	 * reach `introPriceCents` / `introTermMonths` because the symlinked prod Prisma
18	 * client's types predate these columns until it is regenerated at deploy — the
19	 * same stale-client gap `frozenProductAnnualPct` (lib/product-billing.ts) and the
20	 * `Server` writes in lib/order.ts already work around. Identical at runtime once
21	 * the client is regenerated.
22	 */
23	import { termDiscountPct } from "./billing-terms";
24	
25	/** A row that MAY carry the intro columns (present at runtime, absent from stale types). */
26	type PlanIntroFields = { introPriceCents?: number | null; introTermMonths?: number | null };
27	
28	/**
29	 * The plan's intro MONTHLY price in cents, or null when it is unset, malformed, or
30	 * NOT genuinely below the regular price. Requiring `intro < regular` means a bad /
31	 * equal / higher value can never quietly RAISE the first-term charge — it just
32	 * disables the intro and the plan bills its regular price.
33	 *
34	 * `plan` is typed loose on the intro column because the symlinked prod Prisma client's
35	 * types predate it (regenerated at deploy); the value is present at runtime.
36	 */
37	export function planIntroMonthlyCents(plan: { priceCents: number }): number | null {
38	  const v = (plan as PlanIntroFields).introPriceCents;
39	  if (typeof v !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 0) return null;
40	  const cents = Math.round(v);
41	  if (cents >= plan.priceCents) return null;
42	  return cents;
43	}
44	
45	/**
46	 * How many of the first term's months are billed at the intro rate. NULL / invalid
47	 * => the WHOLE first term (returned as null so callers apply it across every month).
48	 * Clamped to >= 1 so a stray 0 can never zero the intro window. `plan` is `unknown`
49	 * for the same stale-client reason as above.
50	 */
51	export function planIntroTermMonths(plan: unknown): number | null {
52	  const v = (plan as PlanIntroFields | null | undefined)?.introTermMonths;
53	  if (typeof v !== "number" || !Number.isFinite(v) || v < 1) return null;
54	  return Math.round(v);
55	}
56	
57	/**
58	 * Cents knocked off the FIRST term because of the intro rate — 0 when there is no
59	 * intro. Expressed as a REDUCTION of the regular term total (not a second price)
60	 * so the regular term price stays the single source of truth and the renewal math
61	 * is untouched:
62	 *
63	 *   discount = (regularMonthly − introMonthly) × introMonths × (1 − termDiscount)
64	 *
65	 * `introMonths` is `min(introTermMonths ?? months, months)`, so a 1-month term is
66	 * fully intro-priced, and a "$3.99 first month" intro on a 12-month first order
67	 * discounts exactly one month and bills the other eleven at the regular rate.
68	 * The term discount is applied so the intro months are discounted consistently
69	 * with the rest of the term the customer chose.
70	 */
71	export function introFirstTermDiscountCents(
72	  regularMonthlyCents: number,
73	  introMonthlyCents: number | null,
74	  termMonths: number,
75	  introTermMonths: number | null,
76	  annualDiscountPct?: number,
77	): number {
78	  if (introMonthlyCents == null || introMonthlyCents >= regularMonthlyCents) return 0;
79	  const months = Math.max(1, Math.round(termMonths));
80	  const introMonths = introTermMonths != null ? Math.min(introTermMonths, months) : months;
81	  if (introMonths <= 0) return 0;
82	  const pct = termDiscountPct(months, annualDiscountPct);
83	  return Math.max(0, Math.round((regularMonthlyCents - introMonthlyCents) * introMonths * (1 - pct / 100)));
84	}
85	
86	/**
87	 * The percent OFF the regular term total that the intro first term represents,
88	 * as a whole number 0..100 — the value stamped on `Server.termPromoPercent` so
89	 * proration and refunds price against the rate the term was actually sold at.
90	 * Integer because it round-trips through Stripe metadata as an integer promo
91	 * percent (lib/order.ts parseOrderPrice), exactly like the seasonal promos.
92	 */
93	export function introSoldPercent(regularTermCents: number, introDiscountCents: number): number {
94	  if (regularTermCents <= 0 || introDiscountCents <= 0) return 0;
95	  return Math.min(100, Math.max(0, Math.round((introDiscountCents / regularTermCents) * 100)));
96	}

253	/**
254	 * The families whose {@link GAME_PORT} entry is deliberately NOT the port a
255	 * player's own game client connects to — mapped to the port that actually is.
256	 *
257	 * `GAME_PORT` is a HEALTH-CHECK map. Where an image exposes a TCP port at all it
258	 * prefers that one, because "a TCP handshake is verifiable with a plain connect,
259	 * and the process binding it is proof the game server itself came up" — see its
260	 * own comment. For most families that port is also the join port, so the
261	 * distinction never mattered. For the eight below it is an RCON/query/admin
262	 * port, and `GAME_PORT`'s own inline comments have always said so.
263	 *
264	 * It started mattering the moment provisioning began auto-forwarding "the game's
265	 * own port" for NAT servers using this same map. Found live 2026-09-06 by
266	 * provisioning a real Rust server on node-2: the guest listened correctly on
267	 * 28015/udp (join) and 28016/tcp (RCON), the node's NAT had exactly one game
268	 * rule — 28016/tcp — and the dashboard handed the customer that RCON port as
269	 * their connect address. No player could ever have joined. That is the identical
270	 * outage found on the real paying customer `rust-w75hko` (see
271	 * docs/DOCUMENTATION.md's node migration section), whose root cause was
272	 * previously read as "allocateGameForward was never called for it"; it is called,
273	 * just with the wrong port.

275	 * Every entry is sourced from the family's own `docker run -p ...` mapping in
276	 * prisma/catalog.ts / the seed-wave*-games.ts files — the only ports docker
277	 * actually exposes off the container — cross-checked against the join port
278	 * `GAME_PORT`'s own comment already names. Anything NOT listed here joins on its
279	 * `GAME_PORT` entry; use {@link joinPortFor} rather than reading this directly.

283	  ark: { port: 7777, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27020/tcp rcon
284	  projectzomboid: { port: 16261, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon
285	  factorio: { port: 34197, protocol: "udp" }, // GAME_PORT is 27015/tcp rcon

 * and the `presence`-driven honesty discipline from) rather than the 40

 *

 * and Falkenstein, Germany (`fsn1`) — see lib/node-regions.ts. Every

export type GamePlanRow = {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  ramMB: number;
  slots: number | null;
  priceCents: number;
  introPriceCents?: number | null;
};

const money = (cents: number) => `$${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;

export function gameFromLabel(plans: GamePlanRow[]): string {
  if (!plans.length) return "$4.99";
  return money(Math.min(...plans.map((p) => planIntroMonthlyCents(p) ?? p.priceCents)));
}

/** Honest "where are the servers" answer for a game-family × location page — direct analogue of locationLandings.ts's serverLocationFaq. */
function gameServerLocationFaq(loc: GameLocationDef, game: string): { q: string; a: string } {
  if (loc.presence === "datacenter") {
    return {
      q: `Is my ${game} server actually hosted in ${loc.name}?`,
      a: `Yes — Nxeon operates a real datacenter that ${loc.slug === "southeast-asia" || loc.slug === "europe" ? `sits inside ${loc.name}` : `is physically in ${loc.name}`}. Your ${game} server runs on genuine local hardware there, close to ${listPhrase(loc.nearby.slice(0, 3))} — we don't market a location we don't run.`,
    };
  }
  if (loc.presence === "network") {
    return {
      q: `Are the ${game} servers physically located in ${loc.name}?`,
      a: `This page is built for the ${loc.audience} ${game} community — not a claim of on-site infrastructure in ${loc.name}. Nxeon's production platform runs from real datacenters in Singapore and Falkenstein, Germany, both genuinely well-connected to ${loc.name}, and you'll deploy to the nearest of the two at checkout. If ${loc.name}-local placement is a hard requirement, our team can confirm the lowest-latency option before you order.`,
    };
  }
  return {
    q: `Does Nxeon have a ${game} server datacenter in ${loc.name}?`,
    a: `No, and we won't pretend otherwise: Nxeon's two real datacenters are in Singapore and Falkenstein, Germany, and neither is close to ${loc.name}. This page targets the ${loc.audience} ${game} audience; at checkout you pick whichever of our two regions gives you the better round-trip, and there's no hidden "local" tier we're not telling you about.`,
  };
}

/** Whether this location can honestly support a "low ping" style claim (datacenter/network) vs an audience-only one (market). */
function canClaimLatency(loc: GameLocationDef): boolean {
  return loc.presence !== "market";
}

export type GameLocationCombo = { location: GameLocationDef; family: GameFamily; slug: string };

export const GAME_LOCATION_COMBOS: GameLocationCombo[] = GAME_LOCATIONS.flatMap((location) =>
  ACTIVE_GAME_FAMILIES.map((family) => ({
    location,
    family,
    slug: `${location.slug}-${GAME_URL_SLUG[family]}-server-hosting`,

export function findGameLocationCombo(slug: string): GameLocationCombo | undefined {
  return GAME_LOCATION_COMBO_BY_SLUG.get(slug);
}

export const GAME_LOCATION_SLUGS: string[] = GAME_LOCATION_COMBOS.map((c) => c.slug);

function gameRelatedLinks(combo: GameLocationCombo): { label: string; href: string }[] {
  const { location: loc, family } = combo;
  const otherLocations = GAME_LOCATIONS.filter((l) => l.slug !== loc.slug)
    .slice(0, 3)
    .map((l) => ({ label: `${l.name} ${gameName(family)} Hosting`, href: `/${l.slug}-${GAME_URL_SLUG[family]}-server-hosting` }));
  return [
    { label: `${gameName(family)} Server Hosting`, href: `/${GAME_URL_SLUG[family]}-server-hosting` },
    ...otherLocations,
    { label: "All game servers", href: "/game-servers" },
    { label: "Pricing", href: "/pricing" },
  ];
}

/**
 * Build the unique landing content for one (game family × location) combo.
 * `plans` is the family's real, active `GamePlan` rows (fetched by the
 * route) — every number quoted below (from-price, RAM range, slot range)
 * comes straight from them.
 */
export function buildGameLocationLanding(
  combo: GameLocationCombo,
  plans: GamePlanRow[],
): BuiltLanding & { gameFamily: GameFamily; productName: string } {
  const { location: loc, family } = combo;
  const game = gameName(family);
  const flavor = GAME_FLAVOR[family];
  const genres = GAME_GENRES[family] ?? [];
  const from = gameFromLabel(plans);
  const near3 = listPhrase(loc.nearby.slice(0, 3));
  const flag = locationFlag(loc);
  const lowPing = canClaimLatency(loc);

  const ramValues = plans.map((p) => p.ramMB).filter((n) => Number.isFinite(n));
  const slotValues = plans.map((p) => p.slots).filter((n): n is number => typeof n === "number");
  const minRamGB = ramValues.length ? Math.min(...ramValues) / 1024 : null;
  const maxRamGB = ramValues.length ? Math.max(...ramValues) / 1024 : null;
  const minSlots = slotValues.length ? Math.min(...slotValues) : null;
  const maxSlots = slotValues.length ? Math.max(...slotValues) : null;

  const sizingLine =
    minRamGB != null && maxRamGB != null
      ? `Plans here range from ${minRamGB % 1 ? minRamGB.toFixed(1) : minRamGB} GB up to ${maxRamGB % 1 ? maxRamGB.toFixed(1) : maxRamGB} GB` +
        (minSlots != null && maxSlots != null ? `, ${minSlots}–${maxSlots} player slots` : "") +
        " — pick the size that matches your group."
      : "Pick the size that matches your group; every tier scales with one click.";

  const pingPhrase = lowPing
    ? `low-ping ${game} servers for ${loc.audience} players`
    : `reliable ${game} servers for the ${loc.audience} community`;

  const metaTitle = `${flag} ${loc.name} ${game} Server Hosting — ${lowPing ? "Low-Ping" : "Managed"} Servers, from ${from}/mo`;
  const metaDescription = `${loc.name} ${game} server hosting for ${loc.regionLong}. ${game} is ${flavor}. Dedicated resources, full file access, DDoS protection and instant setup, from ${from}/mo.`;

  const content = {
    eyebrow: `${flag} ${loc.name} ${game.toLowerCase()} hosting`,
    title: `${pingPhrase[0].toUpperCase()}${pingPhrase.slice(1)} in`,
    highlight: loc.name,
    sub: `Dedicated, game-ready ${game} servers built for ${loc.regionLong} — full file access, DDoS protection and instant setup, from ${from}/mo.`,
    intro: [
      `${game} is ${flavor}. Run one for ${loc.audience} players and the same thing decides whether it feels great or frustrating as any other online game: the round trip between your players and the server. ${loc.hub}`,
      `Nxeon runs ${game} on the same full-root NVMe platform as every other title in the catalog: dedicated CPU and memory per server (no oversold host stealing your tick rate), full file access for mods, plugins and configs, always-on DDoS protection, and instant setup so your world or match is online within minutes.`,
      `This page is tuned for a ${loc.audience} audience across ${near3}${genres.length ? ` looking for a ${genres[0].toLowerCase()}-focused ${game} server` : ""} — deploy, invite your players, and resize with one click as your community grows.`,
    ],
    whyTitle: `Built for ${game} in ${loc.name}`,
    why: [
      { title: lowPing ? `Low ping for ${loc.name}` : `Built for the ${loc.name} audience`, body: lowPing ? `A ${loc.name}-targeted deploy keeps round-trips short for players across ${near3}.` : `Copy, plans and support built around the ${loc.audience} ${game} community, not a generic global template.` },
      { title: "Dedicated resources", body: "Guaranteed CPU and RAM per server on enterprise NVMe — no noisy neighbours eating your tick rate." },
      { title: `Real ${game} ecosystem support`, body: `${game[0].toUpperCase()}${game.slice(1)} is ${flavor} — full file access means you can use it fully, or upload your own configs and mods.` },

/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */
/* General "[Location] VPS/Game Server Hosting" pages — the locations   */
/* from GAME_LOCATIONS that don't already have one via locationLandings */
/* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */

export type GeneralLocationCombo = { location: GameLocationDef; service: Extract<ServiceKey, "vps" | "game">; slug: string };

const GENERAL_SERVICES = SERVICES.filter((s): s is (typeof SERVICES)[number] & { key: "vps" | "game" } => s.key === "vps" || s.key === "game");

export const GENERAL_LOCATION_COMBOS: GeneralLocationCombo[] = GENERAL_PAGE_LOCATIONS.flatMap((location) =>
  GENERAL_SERVICES.map((service) => ({
    location,
    service: service.key,
    slug: `${location.slug}-${service.urlPart}`,
  })),
);

const GENERAL_LOCATION_COMBO_BY_SLUG = new Map(GENERAL_LOCATION_COMBOS.map((c) => [c.slug, c]));

export function findGeneralLocationCombo(slug: string): GeneralLocationCombo | undefined {
  return GENERAL_LOCATION_COMBO_BY_SLUG.get(slug);
}

export const GENERAL_LOCATION_SLUGS: string[] = GENERAL_LOCATION_COMBOS.map((c) => c.slug);

function generalRelatedLinks(combo: GeneralLocationCombo): { label: string; href: string }[] {
  const { location: loc, service } = combo;
  const svcDef = SERVICES.find((s) => s.key === service)!;
  const sibling = service === "vps" ? SERVICES.find((s) => s.key === "game")! : SERVICES.find((s) => s.key === "vps")!;
  return [
    { label: `${loc.name} ${sibling.label}`, href: `/${loc.slug}-${sibling.urlPart}` },
    svcDef.hub,
    { label: "Pricing", href: "/pricing" },
  ];
}

function fromLabelVps(plans: LandingPlan[]): string {
  if (!plans.length) return "$6.49";

#!/bin/bash
# Deploy a ref (default: main from /opt/nxeon) to the staging environment.
# Usage: ./scripts/deploy-staging.sh [git-ref]
set -euo pipefail
REF="${1:-main}"
cd /opt/nxeon-staging

echo "==> Syncing staging to $REF"
git fetch origin
git reset --hard "origin/$REF"

echo "==> Installing dependencies"
npm install --no-audit --no-fund 2>&1 | tail -1

echo "==> Applying database schema"
npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss 2>&1 | tail -2
npm run db:seed 2>&1 | tail -2 || true

echo "==> Building"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4

# next.config sets output:"standalone" but the systemd unit runs the standalone
# server.js directly (not `next start`, which Next.js explicitly does not
# support alongside output:"standalone" — it prints a warning and silently
# fails to resolve some routes, confirmed live 2026-09-10: a brand-new API
# route 404'd under `next start` on this exact build and returned 200 under
# `node .next/standalone/server.js`). The standalone output does NOT include
# public/ or .next/static/ (Next's own documented behavior) — copy them in
# fresh every build, or every static asset/route added after the last copy
# is missing until the next deploy happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static
cp -r public .next/standalone/public
cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
# geoip-lite is in next.config.ts's serverExternalPackages (kept OUT of the JS
# bundle on purpose, since it reads .dat files off its own package path at
# runtime) — but the standalone output tracer only copies files it can trace
# as JS-imported, so an externalized package's own non-JS data files are

# with an uncaught ENOENT the moment the systemd unit ran the standalone

#!/bin/bash
# Promote the currently deployed staging commit to production.
# Verifies staging is healthy, fast-forwards nothing (prod working tree IS the repo),
# then rebuilds + restarts production services.
set -euo pipefail

STG_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon-staging rev-parse HEAD)
PROD_COMMIT=$(git -C /opt/nxeon rev-parse HEAD)

echo "==> Staging is at:    $STG_COMMIT"
echo "==> Production is at: $PROD_COMMIT"

if ! systemctl is-active -q nxeon-staging-web; then
  echo "Refusing to promote: staging web service is not running." >&2

content.content:
echo "==> Building production"
npm run build 2>&1 | tail -4
# Guard: never restart into an incomplete/failed build. A valid production build
# always writes .next/BUILD_ID; if it's missing the build failed mid-way and the
# old in-memory process is still serving — abort rather than kill it.
if [ ! -s /opt/nxeon/.next/BUILD_ID ]; then
  echo "BUILD FAILED: .next/BUILD_ID missing — NOT restarting (old process left serving)." >&2
  exit 1
fi
# next.config sets output:"standalone"; the standalone server.js is what the
# systemd unit actually runs (not `next start` — see deploy-staging.sh's own
# comment on this same step for the 2026-09-10 incident). Its output does NOT
# include public/ or .next/static/ (Next's documented behavior) — refresh
# them every promote, same as staging, or new/changed static assets are
# missing from prod until the next promote happens to also touch this step.
echo "==> Copying static assets into the standalone server output"
rm -rf .next/standalone/public .next/standalone/.next/static
cp -r public .next/standalone/public
cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
# geoip-lite is in next.config.ts's serverExternalPackages (kept OUT of the JS
# bundle since it reads .dat files off its own package path at runtime) — the
# standalone output tracer only copies files it can trace as JS-imported, so
# an externalized package's own non-JS data files are silently left behind.
# Found live 2026-09-10 on staging: this crashes EVERY request with an
# uncaught ENOENT the moment something runs the standalone server.js instead
# of `next start` — geo-ip.ts's own try/catch around geoip.lookup() does NOT
# help, the failure isn't confined to that call. Copy the real data/
# directory every promote, same reasoning as public/.next/static above. This
# has NOT yet bitten production because nxeon-web's systemd unit still runs
# `npm start` (next start) today, not server.js directly — but this fix must
# land before that switch happens, not after.
if [ -d node_modules/geoip-lite/data ]; then
  mkdir -p .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data
  cp -r node_modules/geoip-lite/data/. .next/standalone/node_modules/geoip-lite/data/
fi
# Web runs as the unprivileged 'nxeon' user. .next needs to be writable by it
# (Next cache); the rest stays root-owned and world-readable. .env is the one
# exception: systemd's EnvironmentFile= reads it as root (PID 1, pre-privilege
# drop) so the app's process env is fine either way, but Prisma's generated
# client ALSO opens .env directly at Client instantiation to resolve its own
# env() directives — that read happens as the actual 'nxeon' process user, so
# a root-owned .env throws EACCES there on every cold start (harmless once
# systemd's injected vars are already in process.env, but noisy, and a prior
# root-run edit to this file silently reverted the ownership fix below once
# already — confirmed live 2026-09-02). Keep .env nxeon-owned, not world- or
# group-readable. Do NOT chown the whole tree (breaks root git on .git).
echo "==> Fixing .next/.env ownership for non-root web"
chown -R nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.next 2>/dev/null || true
chown nxeon:nxeon /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
chmod 600 /opt/nxeon/.env 2>/dev/null || true
echo "==> Restarting production web"
systemctl restart nxeon-web

# Drain in-flight provisions before bouncing the worker. Restarting the worker
# mid-provision used to interrupt a live VM build and (with a non-idempotent retry)
# strand the server in ERROR. The start step is now idempotent so this is
# belt-and-suspenders, but avoiding the interruption entirely is cleaner. Bounded
# wait (max ~4 min) so a deploy can never hang forever.
DBURL=$(grep -E '^DATABASE_URL=' /opt/nxeon/.env | head -1 | cut -d= -f2- | tr -d '"')
if [ -n "$DBURL" ] && command -v psql >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  for _ in $(seq 1 24); do
    ACTIVE=$(psql "$DBURL" -tAc "SELECT count(*) FROM \"Job\" WHERE status='RUNNING' AND type='PROVISION';" 2>/dev/null | tr -d '[:space:]')
    [ "${ACTIVE:-0}" = "0" ] && break
    echo "==> Waiting for ${ACTIVE} in-flight provision(s) to finish before restarting worker…"
    sleep 10
  done
fi

echo "==> Restarting production worker"
systemctl restart nxeon-worker
sleep 5
systemctl is-active nxeon-web nxeon-worker
CODE=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://127.0.0.1/)
echo "==> Production responds: HTTP $CODE"
[ "$CODE" = "200" ] || { echo "PRODUCTION UNHEALTHY — check journalctl -u nxeon-web"; exit 1; }
echo "==> Production promote complete"

content.text:
## Summary

Built and shipped the full game-family × location SEO landing matrix, reusing the existing `locationLandings.ts` pattern (one route, one data table, real DB-fed pricing) instead of the 40-hand-file per-game pattern.

**New/changed files** (all absolute paths under `/opt/nxeon`):
- `lib/marketing/gameLocationLandings.ts` — new module: 15-location table (country/region granularity), the honesty `presence` field per location, flags, the 41 qualifying game families, per-family flavor text, and the two builder functions (`buildGameLocationLanding`, `buildGeneralLocationLanding`).
- `app/(marketing)/[slug]/page.tsx` — rewritten to resolve a slug against four tables in order (region → city → general-new-location → game-family) before 404, fetching real `db.plan` or real `db.gamePlan` (with `basePlan` for bandwidth/storage) per slug type.
- `app/sitemap.ts` — added the two new slug loops.
- `lib/marketing/locationLandings.ts` — exported `BuiltLanding` and `listPhrase` so the new module can reuse them (no copy-paste of the honesty logic).
- `components/marketing/PricingGrid.tsx` / `components/marketing/UseCaseLanding.tsx` — added `service`/`gameFamily` props. **Found and fixed a real bug in the process**: every "Deploy now" button was hardcoded to `service="vps"`; a game-family page would have sent a `GamePlan.id` through the VPS `?plan=` param, which is wrong. Verified via live rendered HTML on staging before promoting.

**Page count**: 41 active game families (`ACTIVE_FAMILIES` verified live against `db.gamePlan` — 42 had an active plan, `stationeers` excluded for the same "doesn't actually start" reason `app/sitemap.ts` already excludes it) × 15 locations = **615 game-location pages**, plus **24 general pages** (12 locations × VPS/Game-Server — Singapore/Germany/Europe skipped since they already have one). **639 new pages total.**

**Examples verified live on production** (fresh content, real pricing):
- `https://nxeon.cloud/singapore-minecraft-server-hosting` → 🇸🇬, "from $4.99/mo" (real Minecraft GamePlan intro price), "Nxeon operates a real datacenter... physically in Singapore."
- `https://nxeon.cloud/united-states-rust-server-hosting` → 🇺🇸, "Managed Servers, from $12.99/mo" — honest market-only framing: "neither is close to United States... you pick whichever of our two regions gives you the better round-trip."
- `https://nxeon.cloud/north-america-vps-hosting` → 🌐 (globe fallback, documented in-code as a deliberate choice since no single flag represents the aggregate).

**Flags**: confirmed rendering (`lib/flag-emoji.ts`'s `flagEmoji()`) for all 15 locations; Southeast Asia and Europe use Singapore's/Germany's flag respectively (real DC sits inside each), North America falls back to 🌐.

**Build/deploy**: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean both before and after the bug fix. `scripts/deploy-staging.sh main` succeeded (HTTP 200), verified real content + correct deploy links (`?product=game&family=minecraft&tier=<realGamePlanId>`) before promoting. `scripts/promote-production.sh` succeeded: prod `BUILD_ID` went from `v0R14AaRVsyud1hzAQuE6` → `7-Ibx9KM9naTBw7ZZ-5TK`, services active, HTTP 200, and `https://nxeon.cloud/sitemap.xml` (1247 entries) includes the new URLs. Two commits landed on `main` (`840c8f10f8`, `491252c385`).
